newsitem.title: USA: Mexico consensus building main challenge -- S&P.
newsitem.headline: Mexico consensus building main challenge -- S&P.

text.p: Standard and Poor's will be watching how Mexico's ruling party deals with the need to share power with the opposition, an S&P analyst said Friday.

Lacey Gallagher, director of Latin American sovereign ratings at S&P, said Mexico must develop political consensus and maintain a responsible economic program in order to win an upgrade of its BB long-term foreign currency debt rating.
"Over the next couple of years, the extent and degree of cooperation will critically determine the prospects for the year 2000," Gallagher said at the Americas Society here.

In Sunday's election, the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) lost its absolute majority in the lower house of Congress, where the conservative National Action Party (PAN) and the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) gained ground.

Gallagher said that political and economic frictions could arise as the opposition parties assert themselves and the PRI reflects on its weakened position, particularly as the presidential elections approach in 2000, she said.
"Even transitions within the (PRI) have provoked very profound trauma (in the past)," Gallagher said.
She outlined two major long term risks to economic progress, the first being that discontent with wages could build into a strong backlash against PRI rule in 2000.
"The major uncertainty is how the PRI will react to this potential loss of power," she said.
The current economic plan depends in part on consumption growing more slowly than other components of GDP and real wage growth remaining weak, she said.
Many voters demonstrated their dissatisfaction with the program at the ballot box.
Another threat could stem from consumption building more swiftly than expected, leading to balance of payments problems, the analyst said.
